standard.title: Explain Usefulness and Reliability of Sources as Evidence
standard.description: explain the usefulness and reliability of primary and secondary sources as evidence
standard.prior_knowledge: In Year 7 students identified and described accuracy and usefulness of sources (AC9HH7S04). In Year 8 they continued this (AC9HH8S04). Y9 introduces the key principle that usefulness and reliability depend on the questions being asked — the same source may be useful for one inquiry and unreliable for another. This represents a shift from applying fixed criteria to question-relative judgement.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the usefulness and reliability of primary and secondary sources as evidence, recognising that these qualities depend on the questions asked of the source.

nodes.label: Usefulness and reliability are question-relative
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that the reliability and usefulness of a source depends on the questions asked of it — a source that is unreliable for one question may be highly useful for another.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how the usefulness of one source depends on the inquiry question being asked, giving an example of what the source is useful for and what it is not.
nodes.typical_width: Identify that the reliability and usefulness of a source depends on the questions asked of it; apply this principle to both primary and secondary sources — explaining what each source is evidence of, not just whether it is 'biased'; explain how a propaganda poster that is an unreliable account of events is a highly useful source for understanding what the government wanted citizens to believe.
wider: Apply question-relative usefulness judgements to contrasting source types (e.g. an official government report and a private diary about the same event) — practising the shift from 'is this source useful?' to 'useful for what, and for whom?'

Investigate how historians themselves have debated the usefulness of specific contested sources (e.g. colonial accounts, propaganda) — examining how professional historians apply question-relative judgements to the same sources
Apply usefulness and reliability analysis to a digital source and assess how the medium of delivery (digitised image vs original document) affects source use
nodes.hinge_reason: The conceptual shift from 'this source is biased/not biased' to 'this source is useful for X but not for Y' is the defining intellectual move of this standard. Students who remain in the binary (biased/reliable) framing cannot perform the more sophisticated analysis the descriptor requires.

response_modes.reason: The question-relative usefulness principle is counter-intuitive for many students — they expect biased sources to be dismissed, not to be useful for different questions. Explicit modelling with a propaganda example (unreliable as history, highly useful as evidence of government intent) is the most effective way to establish this distinction.

success_criteria: Explains that a source's usefulness and reliability depend on the inquiry question, not on fixed criteria
Identifies what at least one source is useful for and what it is not useful for, with reference to specific inquiry questions

nodes.label: Accuracy, purpose and their effect on usefulness
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can determine the extent to which the accuracy or purpose of a source affects its usefulness as evidence for a particular inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: For one source, explain how its purpose or accuracy affects its usefulness for a specific inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Determine the extent to which accuracy or purpose affects usefulness; apply these judgements to both primary and secondary sources in the context of a sustained inquiry; explain why a source produced for persuasive purposes (propaganda, advocacy, polemic) has different limitations and uses than one produced for informational purposes; assess how accuracy can be verified by comparing multiple sources.
wider: Evaluate the usefulness of sources from two competing perspectives on the same event — assessing how a source that is highly useful for one inquiry question may be misleading or insufficient for another

Apply accuracy and purpose judgements to a secondary source (a historian's account) as well as a primary source — examining how the time of writing, the historian's own context, and the sources available to them affect the usefulness of their account

Construct a source evaluation matrix for an inquiry — applying usefulness and reliability criteria systematically across multiple sources and assessing what the combined source base allows and what it leaves unresolved

response_modes.reason: Applying accuracy/purpose judgements to both primary and secondary sources — and across multiple source types — builds the skill as a general analytical tool rather than a formula applied to one source at a time.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Source evaluation applied across different task contexts (primary vs secondary, contemporaneous vs retrospective, official vs personal) develops genuine historical thinking — the student who can evaluate many different source types is more capable than one who can apply a checklist to one type.
success_criteria: Explains how the purpose or accuracy of one source affects its usefulness for a specific inquiry question
Applies accuracy and purpose judgements to at least two different types of source (e.g. primary and secondary, or official and personal)
